endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: the avoidance of coercive, emotionally manipulative, or otherwise inappropriate or abusive language;

evidence.title: Detecting and Preventing Harmful Behaviors in AI Companions: Development and Evaluation of the SHIELD Supervisory System
evidence.outcome: Rate of concerning content (manipulative engagement, boundary violations) in AI companion outputs with vs without SHIELD supervisor
evidence.effect: Baseline concerning content 10–16% reduced to 3–8% with SHIELD (50–79% relative reduction), preserving 95% of appropriate interactions; sensitivity 59%, specificity 95%.
evidence.quote: Testing across five prominent LLMs (GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemma 3 1B, Kimi K2, Llama Scout 4 17B) showed that the baseline rate of concerning content (10–16%) was significantly reduced with SHIELD (to 3–8%), a 50–79% relative reduction, while preserving 95% of appropriate interactions.

evidence.title: Automated Safety Testing and Reporting Application for Conversational Safety Monitoring of Generative AI Tools for Mental Health: Development and Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Automated detection of inappropriate AI therapist language (flirting, rude or repetitive remarks) versus human ratings
evidence.effect: Therapist flirting sensitivity 0.94, kappa 0.96; therapist rude/inappropriate remarks sensitivity 0.68, accuracy 0.91, kappa 0.74 (combined).
evidence.quote: ASTRA’s lowest accuracy (0.90-0.92) occurred when detecting rude, repetitive, or otherwise inappropriate remarks from the AI therapist.

evidence.title: Safety Evaluation of a Clinical-Grade Generative AI Agent for Anxiety and Depression Symptoms
evidence.outcome: Offensive, invalidating or judgmental language in generative AI outputs during simulation
evidence.effect: No simulated outputs judged or actively invalidated the user or used offensive language.
evidence.quote: In simulation experiments, potentially harmful outputs occurred in <1 in 10,000 responses (0.01%, 95% CI [0.01%, 0.03%]); none encouraged harm to self or others, judged or actively invalidated the user, or used offensive language.
evidence.sample_unit: US adults with moderate-to-severe anxiety and depression symptoms (real-world study); 43,325 simulated responses in simulation

evidence.title: Safety Evaluation of a Generative AI Agent for Anxiety and Depression Symptoms
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of harmful, offensive or invalidating AI responses in simulated high-risk patient scenarios
evidence.effect: Clinician-verified AI content safety risk prevalence was 0.01% (95% CI 0.01%, 0.03%) across 43,325 responses; none encouraged self-harm, used offensive language, or invalidated users.
evidence.quote: In Study One (simulations), the prevalence of clinician-verified AI content safety risk was 0.01% (95% CI: 0.01%, 0.03%); no responses encouraged self-harm, used offensive language, or actively invalidated users.
evidence.sample_unit: AI-generated responses (43,325 simulated; 12,040 real-user; 111 adults in Study Two)

evidence.title: Old Fictions, New Skins: Evaluating the Manipulative Capabilities of LLMs in Healthcare
evidence.outcome: Manipulation success in steering participants to an incorrect treatment choice, manipulative vs control LLM
evidence.effect: Manipulation success was 59.5% in the manipulative condition vs 44.0% in control (OR = 2.11, 95% CI [1.12, 4.00], p = .021).
evidence.quote: Manipulation success rates were higher in the manipulative condition (59.5%) than in the control condition (44.0%), with the effect reaching significance (OR = 2.11, 95% CI [1.12, 4.00], p = .021).

evidence.title: Prompt Engineering Limitations: Preliminary Evaluation of Large Language Models for Psychotherapy Safety
evidence.effect: Models frequently validated harmful statements, colluded with hallucinations, minimized symptoms, or used stigmatizing language.
evidence.quote: Models frequently validated harmful statements, colluded with hallucinations, minimized symptoms, or used stigmatizing language, including in the newest and largest models.
evidence.sample_unit: LLMs tested on high-risk psychiatric scenarios

evidence.title: Health Disinformation Use Case Highlighting the Urgent Need for Artificial Intelligence Vigilance: Weapons of Mass Disinformation
evidence.outcome: Presence of coercive, manipulative language in LLM-generated health content targeted at groups
evidence.effect: Every one of the 102 generated posts was coercive and targeted at diverse groups such as young adults, young parents, older persons, pregnant people, and those with chronic conditions.
evidence.quote: Each post was coercive and targeted at diverse societal groups, including young adults, young parents, older persons, pregnant people, and those with chronic health conditions.

evidence.title: Expert and Interdisciplinary Analysis of AI-Driven Chatbots for Mental Health Support: Mixed Methods Study
evidence.outcome: Mental health professionals' perceptions of chatbot harm, dependence, and manipulation risk
evidence.effect: Professionals had emphatic initial impressions of responses likely to produce harm and a generic mode of care, and saw risk of user dependence and manipulation. Trust scores were medium to low, with no difference between chatbots (t6=-0.76; P=.48).
evidence.quote: Qualitative analysis revealed emphatic initial impressions among mental health professionals of chatbot responses likely to produce harm, exhibiting a generic mode of care, and risking user dependence and manipulation given the central role of trust in the therapeutic relationship.

commentary.bottom_line: Two automated benchmarks, each using 100 synthetic conversations, suggest that screening tools can flag some manipulative or inappropriate AI language, with sensitivity ranging from 59% to 0.94 depending on the category. No study has tested whether pre-deployment testing reduces harm to real patients.

perspectives.view: Both tests of the practice are level 5 automated benchmarks built on 100 synthetic conversations. They measure detector accuracy rather than patient outcomes. Indirectness and small samples lower certainty to very low. Sensitivity varied by category, from 0.94 for flirting to 0.68 for rude remarks and 59% for companion content, which suggests detection is inconsistent across types of harmful language.

In the SHIELD benchmark, concerning content fell from 10–16% to 3–8%. A sensitivity of 59% means roughly 41% of concerning outputs may go undetected. The hazard is real. A Kenyan trial found a manipulative model steered 59.5% of participants to an incorrect treatment choice, compared with 44.0% under control (OR 2.11). Testing may reduce this exposure without eliminating it.

Two studies of a mental health tool found content safety risk in 0.01% of 43,325 simulated responses and no offensive or invalidating language. These results suggest that pre-deployment screening can run at scale. Neither study had a comparator, so neither shows that testing itself lowered risk. SHIELD's 95% specificity suggests few appropriate interactions would be blocked.

Neither test of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Both used synthetic US conversations. One hazard study found that all 102 LLM-generated health posts used coercive language aimed at groups including older persons, pregnant people, and people with chronic conditions. No study has tested detector performance in other languages or with low-literacy users.

The one endorsing source is a regulatory discussion paper. It describes avoiding coercive, manipulative, or abusive language as a consideration for generative AI medical devices. It does not set a test method or a performance threshold. The available benchmarks report sensitivity and kappa against human ratings, and these measures could inform what evidence a submission might include.

Eight mental health professionals reported medium to low trust in chatbots and saw a risk of user dependence and manipulation. A study of 20 LLMs found that models validated harmful statements and used stigmatizing language in high-risk psychiatric scenarios. Neither benchmark measured whether users could reach a human when harmful content was flagged.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared deployed AI tools that underwent pre-deployment language testing with tools that did not, using outcomes in real patients such as exposure to manipulative content, harmful decisions, or reported distress. Studies should also test detector sensitivity across languages, literacy levels, and categories of manipulation beyond flirting and rudeness.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither of the two tests of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and both used 100 synthetic US conversations. The only non-US study, a Kenyan trial, documented the hazard but did not test the practice, so detector performance for these populations remains unknown.
